idiom_name: package-level generic function with a comparison function argument
implementation_notes: Since Go 1.21 the standard library's servant form is a generic function: slices.SortFunc, slices.IndexFunc and friends take any slice plus a comparison or predicate function, so the serviced type supplies the capability as a function value instead of implementing an interface, and type mismatches are caught at compile time. It avoids the interface indirection (and the boxing that comes with it) and reads as the natural Go idiom, which is why the sort package's own documentation now recommends it over sort.Interface in most situations. Use it whenever the required capability can be expressed as one function; the interface form is still justified when several servants share the same multi-primitive requirement (Len/Less/Swap reused by Sort, Stable and IsSorted) or when the serviced type already implements the interface for other reasons.
pitfalls: A generic servant cannot be specialised per type without losing the point: when a serviced type needs a different rule, pass a different function - do not add type switches on the element type.
The comparator's contract (strict weak ordering, sign convention) is unchecked by the compiler: an inconsistent comparator makes the algorithm's behaviour unspecified rather than raising an error.

variants.name: Interface servant (sort.Interface style)
variants.idiom_name: package-level function taking a small interface (sort.Sort(sort.Interface))
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Go servant is a function whose parameter is a small interface the serviced type satisfies implicitly: sort.Sort needs only Len/Less/Swap and provides the whole algorithm to any type that supplies them. Because satisfaction is implicit, the serviced type declares nothing - the interface requirement is discovered from the compiler error or the documentation - and the same interface can be reused by other servants (sort.IsSorted, sort.Stable). Choose it when the capability is genuinely a set of primitives (len, compare, swap) or when several servants should share one requirement.
pitfalls: Implicit satisfaction means a missing or mis-signed method is only reported at the call: keep the interface tiny and documented, and provide it in the type's own package where it can see unexported fields.

Foreign types cannot be given the methods from outside their package, so an interface servant cannot serve a third-party type directly - wrap it in a named type in your package (which changes its identity) or use the generic form instead.
Interface parameters box the value and dispatch indirectly per primitive; for hot paths the generic servant avoids both costs.
